new_title: Winter rains deepen Gaza crisis amid restricted access and aid cuts
old_text:
Winter rains deepen Gaza crisis amid restricted access and aid cuts
Gaza is facing a deepening shelter, sanitation and food security crisis as winter rains flood makeshift shelters, destroy scarce food supplies and leave displaced families struggling to stay warm and fed.
"Most people burn rubbish to cook their food. Now even the rubbish is wet," warned Shaun Hughes, World Food Programme (WFP) country director for Palestine.
Briefing journalists in Geneva on his visit to the Strip last week, he described how floodwater and sewage had destroyed food stocks stored in tents while cooking gas and firewood are unavailable or unaffordable.
The scale of the damage has increased fears about how displaced families will withstand the winter months ahead.
"After just one day of rain, tens of thousands of shelters were damaged or destroyed," said Karl Baker, regional crisis coordinator for the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM).
At least five people were killed by a collapsed sand bank just over a week ago and humanitarian partners reported that two children had died in fires started accidentally by families trying to stay warm by cooking inside their tents, Mr. Baker added.
Massive displacement
The UN's food and migration agencies warn that critical funding shortfalls and continued restrictions on humanitarian aid deliveries are putting additional pressure on an already fragile response. More than 1.7 million Gazans remain displaced and 1.4 million face acute hunger.
In the tented camps for displaced families, WFP used to provide one hot meal a day.
"Now it's one hot meal every two days,"insisted Mr. Hughes.
'Does not feel like a ceasefire'
The agencies warned that recent improvements in food security remain precarious, sustained mainly by humanitarian aid rather than any recovery in livelihoods, markets or local food systems. Winter flooding and the destruction of food stocks risk reversing those gains.
"When you're in Gaza, it does not feel like a ceasefire," the WFP official stressed. "Israeli military control across nearly 70 per cent of Gaza means that people have almost no space to grow their own food. Fishing in the sea is prohibited and also life-threatening. Unemployment is over 80 per cent, so without humanitarian assistance, people have little or no alternate means of survival," underlined Mr. Hughes.
Holding back floodwaters
As winter sets in, one of the most immediate and effective ways to protect displaced families is to improve the management of displacement camps, according to IOM.
Humanitarian teams have worked for months to prepare sites for winter, digging drainage channels, reinforcing pathways and repurposing flour bags as sandbags to limit flooding.
But, these efforts require at least $9 million in the coming months to support flood prevention, fire safety measures, heating points, lighting and emergency site improvements. And access to more resources and basic tools such as shovels, sandbags and nails is urgently needed to help communities protect themselves and strengthen their shelters.
Humanitarian agencies work closely with Israel's Coordination of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) to ensure that the equipment entering Gaza meets Israeli's security requirements. Clearance takes a long time and is heavily bureaucratic, UN agencies say,
IOM is urging Member States to use their influence with the Israeli authorities to secure the opening of additional crossing points and ensure the immediate and predictable entry of humanitarian supplies, including more robust and longer-lasting shelter equipment.
Any help is welcome
"Anything that can come in at any time, we just highly appreciate it and from any source; but of course, it needs to be durable and that's what we're looking for in order just to get through this winter," said Karl Baker, Head of IOM's Gaza programme.
He noted that IOM has more than 100,000 tents standing by for delivery from Egypt, but securing entry for such essential items depends on strict criteria being met, including the diameter of central tent poles.
"Usually anything under 38 millimetres is okay; anything above, it's usually deemed as not acceptable," he explained. "It is not a statement of dual use, it is just that this tent at this time is not allowed to enter Gaza...We don't get the specifics."

One in four households in Gaza is headed by a woman, and even before the floods, these households were more likely to be living in inadequate shelters.
Widows and women whose husbands have been forcibly disappeared, severely injured or remain missing face "unimaginable hardship, often alone", the agency said.
